title: Gorgias (part 1): Socrates on rhetoric as flattery and why doing wrong is worse than suffering it
summary: Socrates cross-examines Gorgias and Polus on what rhetoric is, arguing it persuades the ignorant without knowledge and is a counterfeit of justice. He then argues that doing injustice is the worst evil, and that escaping punishment is worse than being punished, since punishment heals the soul.

principles.text: Being refuted is a gain: being cured of error beats curing another's.
principles.quote: I hold that this is the greater gain of the two, just as the gain is greater of being cured of a very great evil than of curing another.

principles.text: Truth is not settled by majority or reputable witnesses; one honest interlocutor's real assent is enough.
principles.quote: But this kind of proof is of no value where truth is the aim; a man may often be sworn down by a multitude of false witnesses who have a great air of respectability.

principles.text: Rhetoric that persuades without knowledge is a counterfeit of justice, aimed at pleasure rather than the soul's good.
principles.quote: Rhetoric, according to my view, is the ghost or counterfeit of a part of politics.

principles.text: Real power means doing what is good for you; acting on mistaken opinion about the good is not power.
principles.quote: they do literally nothing which they will, but only what they think best.

principles.text: Doing injustice is the greater evil, so it is better to suffer wrong than to commit it.
principles.quote: I should not like either, but if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do.

principles.text: The unpunished wrongdoer is most miserable; just punishment heals the soul like medicine.
principles.quote: the doer of injustice is more miserable than the sufferer; and he who escapes punishment, more miserable than he who suffers.
